source: Oracle face study 2026-10-23: public knowledge of each game, in our own words; no captures, no game files. Confidence is per row.

techniques.blendshape: Blendshapes (morph targets): the face mesh is sculpted into many shapes (smile, brow raise, jaw open) and the game mixes them by weight. Often driven by performance capture of an actor.
techniques.bone: Bone face: small joints inside the head move the brows, lids, jaw and lips. Cheaper than blendshapes, easy to share between characters, and the usual way stylised games animate faces.
techniques.swap: Texture or sprite swap: the eyes, brows and mouth are drawn as a small sheet of frames and the game swaps between them, like the mouth charts of cartoons.
techniques.decal: Decals and emotes: blush, sweat, tears, sparkles, anger marks and bubbles laid on or over the face. They exaggerate a feeling the face alone can't carry at the distance.
techniques.faceless: Faceless: a helmet, visor, mask, blank doll or tiny figure. The body, the voice, the walk and the camera do all the acting.
techniques.portrait: Dialogue portraits: the in-world figure stays small; a large painted portrait beside the words changes expression per line.

games.what: Actor performance capture on dense face rigs; conversations, horse rides and camp life all keep the face working.
games.why: The camera often sits near the face and the story leans on silence, so the smallest brow move carries meaning.
games.lesson: When the camera comes close, the eyes and brows matter more than the mouth.

games.what: Captured performances for cutscenes; a lighter shared face set for the crowd.
games.why: Two budgets: heroes get the expensive face only when the camera can see it.
games.lesson: Spend the face budget where the camera is; the crowd emotes with the body.

games.what: Procedural lip sync and expression generated from the recorded voice and script tags, so every dubbed language moves the mouth.
games.why: Thousands of lines in many languages; hand animation would never cover them all.
games.lesson: The voice and the script's emotion tags can drive the face automatically. This is the model for our live voices.

games.what: Large amounts of dialogue animated with a mostly automatic pipeline; at launch, stiff eyes and odd expressions became famous.
games.why: It shows what goes wrong: realistic faces with weak eye life fall into the uncanny valley fast.
games.lesson: Blinks, eye darts and a held thought are not optional. Stylised beats realistic when the budget is small.

games.what: One man's many alternate selves share a face; personality shows in how each one holds it.
games.why: Same mesh, different resting mood, posture and voice reads as a different person.
games.lesson: Mood is a resting pose, not a moment. Our FaceDriver keeps a mood under every expression.

games.what: Elizabeth's big, stylised eyes and constant reactions to what you do and see.
games.why: A companion who notices things makes the world feel alive; stylised proportions make her readable from first person.
games.lesson: Big eyes and reactions to the world beat realistic skin.

games.what: Comic-ink faces with a shared library of expressions and gestures, triggered per dialogue line.
games.why: A small team can 'direct' every line by picking an expression and a gesture.
games.lesson: A named expression library per line is enough for a whole story game.

games.what: The same per-line expression and gesture library, with stronger lighting on the face.
games.why: Light and a held expression do the drama; the mouth just needs to sync.
games.lesson: Hold an expression a beat after the line ends; that is where the feeling lands.

games.what: Animated-show style faces with snappy, pose-to-pose expressions in conversation.
games.why: Cartoon timing (quick change, long hold) reads better than smooth realism.
games.lesson: Snap into an expression in about a tenth of a second, then hold.

games.what: Disney-style faces, plus emotes and animated reactions when you talk to characters.
games.why: Kids already know these faces; strong brows and wide mouths read at game camera distance.
games.lesson: Feature-film shape language (round, readable, exaggerated) works in a game camera.

games.what: Faces built to match the show's 2D drawings: simple eyes and mouth shapes on a 3D head.
games.why: Matching the show's few, clear shapes keeps the characters on-model from every angle.
games.lesson: A small set of clear shapes is better than many subtle ones for kids.

games.what: Show-accurate pup faces, with cheerful idle expressions and lip sync for the cast's lines.
games.why: Young players read big eyes and open smiles instantly.
games.lesson: For little kids, the default face should already be friendly.

games.what: Source engine face 'flexes': each class has exaggerated brows, grins and grimaces; voice lines carry their own expressions.
games.why: Caricature plus a voice line makes each class a character even in a shooter.
games.lesson: Exaggerate the face for the distance it is seen at.

games.what: Players pose Source characters' faces with sliders (the face poser) to make comics and scenes.
games.why: Giving players the face sliders turns expression into a toy.
games.lesson: Expressions can be a puppet toy for kids, not just playback. Our 2D puppet should expose them.

games.what: Kerbals' faces react to the flight: grins, panic and wide eyes in the crew portraits, shaped by each kerbal's courage and stupidity.
games.why: The simulation drives the face, so their expression tells you how the flight is going.
games.lesson: Let game state drive the face. Feelings come from what is happening, not a script.

games.what: Duplicants' cartoon faces and whole-body stress reactions (crying, tantrums) show how the colony is doing.
games.why: In a management game you read mood at a glance across the whole base.
games.lesson: At a distance, a body reaction beats a subtle face.

games.what: LEGO minifigure faces are printed; expression changes by swapping the printed face, and the body hops and waves.
games.why: It keeps the toy honest: a real LEGO face can't stretch.
games.lesson: Texture swap keeps a toy look truthful; this is our painted mode.

games.what: Cut-out 2D animation: eyes and mouths are drawn parts swapped and squashed; followers show emotes over their heads.
games.why: Cute shapes plus quick swaps make it read as a cartoon, even when the content is dark.
games.lesson: Cut-out parts plus a swap sheet is a fast, charming pipeline. It fits our 2D puppet.

games.what: Hand-drawn cut-out characters whose faces swap between drawn frames; voices are instrument mumbles.
games.why: Style plus a non-word voice keeps it universal and cheap to localise.
games.lesson: A mumble voice with a swap face is a whole character with no lip sync needed.

games.what: Paper cut-out faces with mouth frames swapped exactly like the show.
games.why: Copying the show's crude method makes the game look exactly like the show.
games.lesson: The 'worse' technique is right when it matches the look.

games.what: 2D cut-out plants and zombies with simple animated faces and big, bouncy body loops.
games.why: On a lawn of dozens, the bounce tells you what each one is doing.
games.lesson: Idle rhythm is part of the face when the character is small.

games.what: Small figures in play; large painted portraits beside dialogue swap expression per line.
games.why: The isometric figure can't show a face, so the portrait does it, only when someone talks.
games.lesson: Summon the face when it is needed instead of shrinking it into the world.

games.what: Painted crew portraits whose expressions show morale while you make hard choices.
games.why: The portrait is the crew's mood meter, read as faces, not numbers.
games.lesson: A face can replace a number.

games.what: Pixel portraits at the booth window; small changes (a smile, a glance) are the drama.
games.why: With so few pixels, one changed pixel of mouth carries a lot.
games.lesson: Tiny faces need one big, clear change, not many small ones.

games.what: Pixel-art characters with extravagant hand-animated cutscene reactions.
games.why: Over-the-top reactions are the comedy; the pixel art keeps them cheap.
games.lesson: Big comic reactions can be authored as short sprite clips.

games.what: Pixel characters change their face sprite for emotes, including from typed chat emoticons.
games.why: Typing a smiley makes your character smile: the line drives the face.
games.lesson: Text drives the face. Our [tags] are the same idea for voice lines.

games.what: Top-down pawns show their mood with thought bubbles and mental-state text instead of faces.
games.why: At that zoom, a face is a few pixels; a bubble isn't.
games.lesson: Below a certain size, switch from face to a spatial bubble.

games.what: Crewmates have a visor and no face; emotion comes from walk, colour, voice chat and the meeting screen.
games.why: Hiding the face is the game: you can't read who is lying.
games.lesson: No face can be a design choice. The body and the voice still emote.

games.what: Helmets hide faces; salutes, hugs, high-fives and shouted callouts carry the feeling.
games.why: Gestures you trigger yourself become the social language.
games.lesson: A small gesture wheel is a face for helmeted characters (Moon base heroes).

games.what: Astronauts behind visors; emotes and body language do the talking.
games.why: Cute proportions plus big gestures read even with no face.
games.lesson: Our Moon astronauts can emote through visor glow and body.

games.what: Blank red crystal figures; their poses and how they shatter are the whole expression.
games.why: Removing faces focuses you on motion and time.
games.lesson: Posing alone carries intent; the wooden mannequin can do this.

games.what: Painted wooden dolls with fixed faces; they act with wobbles and silent-film title cards.
games.why: A painted toy face can't move, so the body and the theatre carry it.
games.lesson: A toy with a fixed face is still expressive if the body acts. Strong fit for Abbie's World toys.

games.what: The Kid's face is tiny; a narrator's voice carries every feeling.
games.why: Voice is a face you hear.
games.lesson: When the face can't read, let a voice react (diegetic, sound grid).

games.what: GLaDOS and the turrets have no faces: a light, a single eye and a voice.
games.why: One glowing eye plus a great voice is a full character.
games.lesson: A single light can be a face (robots, the Moon base).

games.what: A small, nearly blank face; the world's colour and music change with her grief.
games.why: The whole game adapts: one feeling drives light, colour and sound.
games.lesson: Our expression mood (valence, arousal) can also steer music and light.

games.what: Simple dot faces on wobbly physics bodies; the flopping is the comedy.
games.why: Physics makes every reaction fresh and funny.
games.lesson: Physical wobble on reactions keeps faces from looking canned.

games.what: Tiny chefs with minimal faces; panic shows in running, the kitchen and the music.
games.why: The kitchen and the clock carry the stress.
games.lesson: Meta and diegetic stress beat a worried face when characters are small (coffee shop dialect).

games.what: A top-down camera keeps faces small; the actors' voices and bodies carry the thriller.
games.why: The camera choice decides how much face you need.
games.lesson: Choose the camera first, then the face budget.

games.what: The player's real blinks, read by webcam, move the story forward.
games.why: The player's own face becomes the controller.
games.lesson: Powerful, but a kid's camera stays off in Abbie's World: no player-face capture.

games.what: No characters to read; sheep and birds simply behave.
games.why: The world itself shows calm and life.
games.lesson: 'None' is a valid answer: the world behaves differently.
